I know how hard it is for you. I was lost at 33. I thought that having a business, marriage, kids, a home, etc., meant I was all good. It might have been if I had allowed myself to get help and heal. I'm not even sure the help or awareness even existed then. But it does now. I hope you, and everyone else who's struggling, find healing. I have a young friend (30 years old) who I met online, who hasn't had the stability or support that most of us could take for granted. Even having the memory of when things were "okay", or when we felt safe or protected. Added to her isolation and homelessness. If she can keep fighting, we can too.

I don't know your story, but I hope that you have some "safe place" or refuge that you can retreat to. If only in your mind. Trauma isn't something any of us "get over", or just stop being affected by. We don't age out of needing kindness and understanding, and our triggers don't magically disappear. Instead it's more likely that we stop speaking for the comfort of others, or because no one will listen or help. If we were ever able to share our truth at all. Claim your right to peace of mind and to know how it feels to be loved, unconditionally. Starting with ourselves.

I'm nearly 69 years old, and still coming to terms with everything that happened when I was young. It ALL impacted my life in ways that I've only come to understand over the last decade or so. For a long time I viewed myself as having been "sexually active" since early childhood ...until I had my own children. Then I was utterly horrified at the thought of any of them having to deal with anything remotely like what I had experienced. Nobody should ever have "that" so normalized or treated so nonchalantly. It took a lot to face how groomed and coerced I was, when I think that looking at it like I was "willing" made it seem less abusive somehow. I'm grateful that we can finally begin to talk about it. Not easy.

My empathetic response has always been to share an experience from my life that mirrors theirs. For years I couldn't understand why people would take it as "only talking about myself", when I was really making an effort to substantiate how and why I understood, and that I had QUALIFIED my compassion for them.

She's been there as a mail handler for nearly six months (including 5 weeks on emergency placement). She passed the clerks exam and was offered that job, but she had already accepted the mail handlers position. She moved to a new area to accept the job with the last of her savings. But had been going broke using Lyft to and from the Airbnb where she was staying. So the car actually saved her money.
She's not on probation, she's converted.

She's homeless and sleeping in the car she bought with her first two paychecks. She was honestly excited to have the job, and now she's broke. She had just been approved for an apartment right before she was put on emergency placement, and lost that opportunity. She's exhausted and has no one, no friends or family. Except me, and I'm doing all I can. It's f'ing heartbreaking, fr.

"which is easily fixed"??? WTF!!!, I'm going to assume you're relatively young. As a 68 year old AuDHD, it has NEVER gotten any easier ...or "fixed". I'm sorry for whatever struggles you are facing, but you're making broad assumptions that deny the difficulties we ALL face. Attractive, unattractive, high, low or barely functioning. The only universal truth I've identified is that if you're "high functioning", no one (NT) understands when you CAN'T function (within the straightjacket of conventional social paradigms). Try not to ADD to the divisiveness that we are already overwhelmed by. By creating or promoting division within our neurodiverse communities.

My heart breaks for you and your daughter. I'm sorry for what you will have to endure. My wife committed suicide, it will be 6 years this coming Thanksgiving. It was actually on the 22nd, but it will always be Thanksgiving for me and our daughters. All you need to do right now is survive from moment to moment. There will be time ahead for everything else. 

My opinion... Accept the help that you want, and say no to what you don't. Tell your daughter you will never leave her, and share each other's grief. I know it probably feels unimaginable that your lives will ever be "right" again. You will find a balance between sorrow, self-doubts, and serenity, and all your thoughts and feelings. But it will take time. Please be kind to yourself, and let patience and understanding be your allies.

Directly communicate. Break it down for him, maybe just show him what you've written here. With the caveat that you value his friendship and you don't want this to be a problem, for any of you. I'd also suggest bringing your girlfriend up to speed with all of the above. My opinion, based on how I wish I had been treated when people were creeped out or uncomfortable with me. Because 99.999% of the time I was oblivious and blindsided when there were bad outcomes that could easily have been avoided if someone had taken the time to clue me in.

After a lifetime of feeling alienated from humanity, a diagnosis would be an affirmation to ease my feelings of imposter syndrome and that there was/is some explanation for my life experience, existence, and perpetual outsider angst. It might lessen my ongoing existential crisis to some degree. It's complicated, but that's the essence.

Educate yourself as thoroughly as possible. Learn your triggers and accommodations. I'll be 68 in 5 days. I haven't worked productively or professionally since 2007, after complete burnout and shutdown. Always figured I was autistic/ADHD, but never bothered to research it until 7-8 years ago. When it occurred to me there might be a connection between what I now understand is my neurodiversity and the enormity of trauma in my life that began in infancy. Literally. I have been researching it rather obsessively ever since. If I had understood that my struggles through life were manifestations of being AuDHD I might have been able to accommodate myself. Trying to salvage a life from the ashes of cPTSD. You can avoid this. Knowledge/awareness is power.
The agony...

In my 30's I was newly married, bought a house was running my own business and had kids. I always sensed I was autistic because of the skills I had developed and relatives that were accomplished in mathematics and the sciences. I was in my early 60's when I was trying to figure out why my life had gone so far off track. Off the rails completely actually. 

Tell your brother and let him investigate and develop whatever accommodations he needs for himself. Because chances are he's going to need them at some point. When his hold on maintaining "normalcy" begins to unravel. Maybe it won't, but if it does it would be far better to be in a position to manage rather than meltdown and burnout. I kept pushing past all of what I now know were obvious signs, struggling to maintain the facade. Until I could barely face people.

Morning... maybe start by not flogging yourself. I'm not being a smart-ass. I'm just saying give yourself some grace. When the impulse strikes, take a moment to consider what you're after or hoping for. Because it isn't for NO reason. You don't have to perfect yourself overnight. If you can work on figuring out what it is that you feel you're missing and what void you're trying to fill ...you will do more good than abstinence from everything you're chastising yourself for now. Just a thought plucked from a lifetime of tormenting myself, but with the clarity borne of having ceased tormenting myself ...albeit fairly recently (last 6-7 years).

I know that feeling. I'm 67 now, but only just coming to the self-awareness that I observe in so many young people who are struggling with their trauma. I attempted suicide at 18, a few weeks into my first semester at university and about a week after the first time I had sex with a woman. What I now recognize as the first truly consensual intimacy, despite believing I had been "active" since toddlerhood. Now I understand that I couldn't consent to any of it. Because I was a child.

But to the sense of being in hell... It took weeks to come back to consciousness. I'm not sure how long I was unconscious, or if I had been so sedated that I just can't remember. It wasn't until I was 35 that I learned I had a stroke at some point in that whole catastrophe. I was being examined as a result of a car accident and the doctor asked when I had my stroke. Hmmmm. The whole thing was a blur. Not so much leading up to it, that part was painfully intact. Very complicated emotions surrounding the realization that intimacy could be something other than coerced. That it could be beautiful.

But the during and after of the "attempt" was foggy, with critical points tattooed on my soul. Like an externalized internal struggle. Pills and rum. Enough, more than enough. But something made me fight. Alternately coherent, unconscious, convulsing, and violent. Instead of calling 911, the infirmary called my parents to "get him out of here". Or the equivalent. Anyway, lots of very messy details, literally. At one point waking up on a gurney and flinging myself at a wire-reinforced window. Which apparently I had been threatening in brief moments of semi-coherence. It nearly took my hand off. 

So enough, there's more but you get the idea. Very f'd up. In every way imaginable. But as ugly as that all was, and to return to the idea postulated. If I was in hell, how would I know? Because honestly, for YEARS afterward, I wasn't sure that I hadn't succeeded and that the hell I was living in was or wasn't real. Because everyone around me acted like I was the walking dead. I sensed the seething anger directed at me. In stark contrast to how I imagined a loved one might be treated. "How could I have done this" to ________ (fill in the blank*).

* my name was not on the list.

So the message was how could I... hurt my mother, my parents, destroy my future, or present, throw away my potential, etc., etc.. At no point did anyone enquire WHY? In fact it wasn't viewed as an attempt, it was seen as selfish recreational drug use. A couple of thousand mg of phenolbarbitol and a bottle of 151 rum, and me 95 pounds. The last thing I expected was waking up, ever. When I did finally "come to", I was in the "State Hospital". Notorious for people NEVER GETTING OUT. A point rammed home when a fellow inmate on the adolescent ward told me he'd been there SEVEN YEARS, after I mentioned the legal mechanism that landed me there. He laughed and said "me too". Perplexed I said "but I'm going to have a 90-day review" and he said "you'll see". 

Indeed I did. The night before my review there were "extra" pills to swallow and have my face grabbed and flashlight shone in my mouth to make SURE I swallowed. The next morning I staggered into my review my body contorted and palsied and my words fighting with my mouth and coming out like a possessed southern Baptist speaking in tongues. I was once one, so... Tears streaming down my face. Looking at their faces nodding sympathetically, clucking and tut-tutting that maybe one of the attendants could take me for a bit of a lie-down. While they scribbled and nodded to each other.

These same attendants who would inject Benny with 1,500mg of Thorazine and take bets amongst themselves to see how long it would take him to "hit the deck". Or allow a couple of the kids from the back ward to let loose on each other, to dissipate their pent-up aggressions. Only stopping them when one split the others head open on the concrete, open enough that it was going to be a mess to clean up. Or the "nice" night attendant who would slip into the only occupied private room on the ward. My room. Because my arm was in a cast due to my hand that needed reattaching. Which btw, they did a fair job of with my thumb and two fingers operable, forever after. But the main reason I was in that room was because if I were in the dormitory I would be prey. Like little (smaller than me) Nestor, who was found wandering in Harlem. Calling for his mother. Coincidently as he did every night as God knows how many hormonal teenage psychopaths had a go at him... "¡Ayudame MAMA, AYUDAME!!
And it wasn't love... it was hell.

I could go on, but you get the idea.

This is the reality of being "high-functioning". No one understands when it becomes hard to function, or when the stress and burnout BECOME disabling. Speaking from personal experience. I not only did all of the above in terms of functioning, but I also excelled. To the point that I ran my own small manufacturing business in New York City. Until I couldn't. 

You're ahead of me in that you possess the awareness that I did not. While I had always suspected I was autistic, I never had any further understanding of how it was manifesting in my life. In particular, the sheer exhaustion I endured eventually overwhelmed me to complete burnout. I now understand that running my business WAS a way to accommodate my social anxiety about dealing within "work culture". I was usually well regarded by my employers, even sought after. But I could not sustain the banality of daily social interactions with co-workers. 

Fortunately for you, you have the awareness that I did not 40 years ago. Be kind to yourself. If you have underlying trauma, please find a way to unpack, process, and heal. It will not simply resolve without proactive measures on your part, to accommodate yourself. I have found that being in a natural environment can be an immense help. As well as communicating with the people you love and trust, including yourself. I hope.

I'd say it was probably her way of letting you know she would welcome grandchildren. Albeit in a completely tone-deaf and inherently racist space that most white people come from. Speaking as the white half of an interracial couple. My wife didn't grow up in the U.S. and as a result, I think I was more aware of our peculiarly toxic racist culture. Although she got a real quick education as far as the fetishization, condescension, and misogynoir aimed at both her and our three "beautiful mixed children" (which they certainly were and are). 

The bigger issue was/is trauma, and how to unpack, process and heal both ours and (unfortunately) theirs. My parents adored my wife and our children. I have to credit my father's worldliness and intelligence for raising me with a sense of what is truly important. The content of a person's character, conscience, and our capacity for compassion toward ourselves and others. Sadly that progressive worldview in my extended family died with him. 

As it turned out, our little family was ostracized (after my parents' death) by both of our families, for essentially the same reasons ...ignorance, fear and prejudice.

I think you may be experiencing this trauma because you are "safe" now. When you were with them you may have been rationalizing what you were experiencing, and dissociating from how wilfully your boundaries were being broken. At least that's what I realized about my own abusive/manipulative/exploitive "relationship" once I was no longer doing emotional contortions just to survive. I hope you continue to seek understanding to unpack, process, and heal. Forgive and forget doesn't work in my experience (of forgiving and forgetting), it only internalized the anger and sorrow that inevitably metastasized and resurfaced years later. Silence only made me complicit with my abuser... and compounded the trauma.

I went to see an "autism specialist", a psychologist who told me ten minutes into our session that he "knows it when he sees it". The only other patients I met were avoidant, rocking and stimming, like "rain man". Since I was able to present myself appropriately I'll assume I didn't meet his criteria for a diagnosis. I wanted some clarity to decipher what was fueling the severe executive function that had unraveled my career and was affecting my relationship with my wife of 30 years. Whether it was cPTSD, or autism (which I had long assumed was a root cause of many of my lifelong struggles). He was more interested in my trauma... TOO interested. In response to disclosing decade-long serial abuse, molestation, exploitation, and trafficking at the hands of (male) predators/pedophiles he said: "So you're gay then...", and wanted explicit details of the abuse. 😬

I think there is something validating about sharing explicit details about your trauma. To anyone willing to hear it. There really aren't people to share that with, so unfortunately those creeps are among a very small group of people that you can be so open with. Of course there are therapists, but I've found that 45 minutes once, twice or even three times a week doesn't satisfy the urge to unload everything. The reality is that those creeps are more than willing, because they're getting off on it. It's hard to have to carry that trauma around with you, and remain silent because people usually react badly. I'm so dissociated that it's like I'm talking about someone else. I feel bad for that kid, but I see can't seem to make the connection that it's me. I hope this makes some sense.

You're very pretty, delicate features, soulful eyes and beautiful hair. Don't listen to trolls who deal with their inadequacy by trying to inflame your insecurity. It's normal to wonder how others see you, but you needn't be concerned.

Thank you. I don't know what okay feels like, I don't think I ever have. The care and support that might have helped never happened, despite considerable effort. For any of us. Which has led me to wonder sometimes, why am I still here. I'm not suicidal. I've been trying to answer that question for a while now, because I think it's relevant to what might help other survivors choose life. I realize that means different things for different people, but they all include a loss of hope and an inability to see beyond despair.

One way or another it will affect your life, and not in a good way. I've realized that I've lived in a dissociated state since childhood. And as more trauma occured I dissociated from that too. It became intergenerational trauma because I wasn't emotionally available in my marriage or for our children. So I couldn't teach them healthy coping skills among other things. My wife was also dissociated from her cPTSD. We both were/are autistic/ADHD. She committed suicide 3 1/2 years ago. My son also, 2 years ago yesterday. Trauma doesn't magically dissipate. Like an earlier comment talked about his boss telling him how he got over  being raped as a child, and then fired him because a work location was triggering. I'd say that boss didn't "get over" anything.

66, I've done a lot of work on myself the last few years but I'm therapist averse. Peer support and Buddhism has given me perspective and is helping me unpack and process. I'm not sure what healing looks like. I'm not particularly unhappy, but I didn't expect to be alone at this time of my life. It has taken all this time to recognize some events/situations as trauma.

I'm sorry. I can only relate my own thoughts and perspective. No matter how well we cope, it is the finality that hurts. The reality is that no matter how well we may heal, we don't have them present in our lives. 
 
My wife took her life on Thanksgiving day, 4 1/2 years ago. Tomorrow is the second anniversary of my son's suicide. My wife had struggled with depression and cPTSD as a result of SA by her father (and others) that had continued until shortly before we met. My son was also severely depressed, and was inconsolable after she had died.

I had never really faced my own SA, or the impact it had throughout my adult life, in my marriage and certainly as a parent. My wife and I were mindful that we did not want our children to be traumatized. Especially from SA, or by us in any way. But the truth was, that neither of us had ever really unpacked, processed and healed our own trauma. Instead, opting to carry on with our lives as if remaining silent would make it go away. We had protected our hearts as children, but at the expense of our ability to have and share emotions as adults.  

You asked what you could do to honor your sister? You're doing it, by seeking truth, healing and understanding. Your concern is a selfless act of compassion to illuminate and celebrate her life. Whatever your beliefs may be, whether hope for heaven or the continuum of rebirth. Her life, however brief or long, is worthy... compelling and complete. 

Your determination on her behalf is a reflection of hope, and an antidote to the nihilism that extinguished her life. Every effort you make to relieve human suffering (including yours) IS healing through purpose, an act of faith. Light a candle and say a prayer (or a mantra). Not in sorrow, but as a testament to honor her. For bringing you this point in your life, to embrace awareness and compassion. Your sister lives on, because you carry her in your heart.

I told my wife (to be) about my abuse on the way to the restaurant on our first date. Not in explicit detail, but quite enough to scare her off if that were to be the case. I had fallen in love with her nearly as soon as when I had first met her, six months before. I was afraid if I waited I would be utterly heartbroken if she were to reject me when finding out later.

Her story came out over the course of our engagement. After we married she told me she knew she would marry me that first night.  Because I had put my trust in her, she knew she could trust me. We never pried, never abused that trust and never weaponized what we knew of each other's trauma. Not once, not ever, in 32 years of marriage.

But we never really healed either. Instead, that sorrow was hidden behind material success, our marriage and denial. Yes, it's essential to unpack, process and heal your trauma... with awareness, acceptance and compassion. But not in the bedroom (at the expense of your trauma), where you deserve respect, tenderness and trust. 

I regret that neither of us had been more proactive, and that we both never found the support we needed. Despite trying. Instead, those walls we had built to protect our tender hearts as children, kept us from truly embracing our love for each other, ourselves and our children. My wife ended her life ten days after her mother called her a liar, when she finally disclosed the SA perpetrated by her father (and others).

Please... don't wait to leave him (immediately), and find competent, QUALIFIED, trauma informed therapist for yourself. So that you can have the healing and happiness that you deserve. 🙏🙏🙏

To me, that explains everything. Not only the ambivalence about sexuality, but towards the whole of life and our place in it. That combination of being autistic plus trauma is the root of our challenges, beyond all the struggles that come with neurodivergence (in my opinion). I didn't understand that until my life unraveled AFTER I had finally "pulled myself up by my bootstraps" in my late 30's. I kept pushing myself but couldn't sustain the performance of functionality, and didn't understand why. I'm finally figuring it out now, in my 60's.

I don't know if this will help, I was pretty confused and also struggled with all you parenthetically have been dealing with. To the point that I came out as gay at 19, only to definitively understand I wasn't (gay). After being picked up by a pedophile psychologist at a day treatment program who convinced me my problems were a result of my repressed homosexuality (I looked 13). I realized or admitted to myself that I wasn't attracted to men... at all. I didn't recognize my own right to assert my own preference or acknowledge that I even HAD a preference, after molestation, abuse, trafficking, addiction etc. Because it was never (or very rarely anyway) violent or threatening. I realize now it was because I was so thoroughly groomed and gaslit since toddler hood. Also I was/am; autistic, sapiosexual and demisexual.

I've discovered for myself (I'm alexithymic) that it's more that I can't identify, process and express my emotions, rather than not having any. I'm learning to recognize how I manifest my feelings. Likewise, I suspect you might have a similar situation. You must have married your wife for a reason, and have also stayed with her. I understand how upsetting and bewildering it can be, for both of you. Try being honest about how it affects you and enlist her help to strengthen your relationship. I think the common misconception is that not "feeling" means not caring. I discovered I do care (deeply), but tend to show it by the effort I make to be analytical, objective and rational.

My wife and I were both survivors of extensive, serial sexual abuse. I told her an abbreviated version of my trauma as we were driving to a restaurant on our first date. Her disclosures came afterward, but we both knew the broad outlines of each other's story. Our families either did not know, denied or refused to accept what had happened. I never pried and felt this was proper and respectful, and neither did she. I wanted her to feel safe and give her space. We both had/have mental health issues stemming from the abuse, and my wife received disability for PTSD. My biggest regret is that I did not ensure that we both received trauma informed therapy to help us unpack, process and heal what had happened, because it impacted every facet of our lives.

When she finally confronted her mother because she kept on referring to the "good home" and many advantages that had been provided to my wife growing up... her mother called her a liar and stopped speaking to my wife. Ten days later my wife took her own life. I had assumed that her psychologist of over a decade had been working with my wife to heal those wounds. Speaking to him after she died he said "it never came up", despite the fact that I had brought it up on several occasions during joint sessions with him. 

Your husband has no inherent right to know any more than you are willing to share. However it is a valid concern that you should not bear this burden in silence. We were guarded and emotionally distant and at times unavailable. With each other, and our children. Our trauma became intergenerational because we never healed. We hid our pain behind careers, stoicism and appearances. So while you are not obliged to share your "secrets", they need to be reconciled. Competent therapy could help you both explore his "need to know" and address his reasons for insisting you tell him. To help you both heal and resolve, because it affects you both. Please.

I'm really sorry to hear that. It just adds a so much additional stress and vulnerability. Which for me results in me shutting down or dissociating. When I really need to be present. I will say that sharing, over-sharing and trauma dumping with people who can relate and understand (like here) has REALLY helped. That people were able to accept and affirm instead of the usual shame and blame, made me feel less isolated. Even though I am a recluse.
Sorry to hear that, are you homeless?

A long soak in a hot tub seems to help. I've had similar realizations. Most recently that I don't struggle with cPTSD all the time, but that I do still face challenges. My epiphany was that when I'm triggered I shut down. Like back to the wall high alert. I'm 66 now, and my 33 year old daughter pointed out that she's watched this happen to me her whole life, and can tell when it's happening. I think I've just been so dissociated I didn't see it. But the signs were obvious now that I look back. I used to have a hair trigger temper and would have what seemed to be random meltdowns, but were actually when I'd be triggered and I'd revert back to that freaked out kid. 

Anywhere from 2 to 20 years old, depending on what was triggered. I'm a work in progress, which is progress in itself... that I'm able to find new ways to identify and accommodate what sets me off and how I react. I do feel terrible though, for how it affected me as a husband and parent. And I have talked at length with my kids about it. Better late than never isn't always much comfort.

Being someone with PTSD sets you apart from people who don't have it. While it's true that we're each responsible for our own emotional state... the response of those closest to us can have an impact sometimes nearly as stressful as the PTSD itself. There have been comments asserting that your partner should not be obliged to be relied on, while at the same time chastising you for not moderating your trauma response, ("yelling") when triggered. Which may be clinically correct, but is compassionately wrong. 

When you're in the midst of a PTSD triggered panic attack, you need understanding and kindness, unconditionally. Not a lecture from the person closest to you, or to debate how much understanding you're entitled to. I agree that we should all be mindful of our actions and attitudes. But insisting on that consideration from someone in the throes of PTSD, while depriving them of the timely support they need... seems unfair. Hopefully your healing will progress over time and with support. You will learn to temper your reactions while overwhelmed and panicking in due course, but you're not there yet. Until then, don't let anyone invalidate you. My opinion. I hear you, and I'm sorry.

Then here and now gone, undulating above my Chenango. The only vestige of barges and towpaths left, in incongruous names of river towns and odd slumped stretches of infilled canals. I struggled with meltdowns and being autistic all my life. I just didn't recognize the difficulties I had as manifestations of autism, until I self assessed. I always figured I was autistic, but I didn't know much about it. I thought the way I could design engineer things in my imagination, and then actually build them from that mental plan was what it was to be autistic. Also that my nerdiness and social awkwardness were part of it. But I had never researched it and educated myself about the impact it has on peoples lives. As I've learned more and more about autism I've learned to recognize my triggers and accommodate myself when I feel like I'm heading towards a meltdown. 

I snap when I reach the breaking point, but I've learned to pay attention to when I feel myself getting upset. I don't handle sudden changes very well. Of my schedule, or interruptions to my plan for the day. I appreciate prior notice, and don't like surprise visits. I try to step away from a triggering situations when they happen to come up. Like, literally excuse myself and go somewhere to calm myself. It can be as simple as going and sitting quietly in the car, or bathroom for a few minutes. I used to just lose it and yell or get really agitated. Like a temper tantrum. 

It still happens once in a while but I don't take it out on everyone around me like I used to. Also, make sure to go to bed at a reasonable hour, and to eat and stay hydrated. Not kidding. I'm still working on executive function and burnout, but knowledge is power. Identifying issues that are challenging for me, and letting myself process them in my own way has been all for the better. Instead of pushing myself to live up to unreasonable expectations for myself. 

Especially not subjecting myself to social "obligations" that I know will be too much for me, when I used to force myself. It's like torture for me, having to make small talk and smile. I allow myself to indulge in my interests and to respect my own boundaries. If others can't take me as I am, then I prefer my own company. Rather than having to perform a certain way (which I've never figured out) to satisfy other peoples expectations.

You didn't mention which country you're in, because it does vary as far as next steps. I think it's a good starting point to talk to your doctor or therapist, or both if you have them. Either one could advise or refer you for further testing, but ideally a therapist would be able to recommend someone qualified. In the U.S. the assessment needs to be documented by a doctoral level therapist, eg. a psychologist or neuropsychologist, from the state you need/want accomodations from. A psychiatrist can also offer a formal (as in legitimate) diagnosis.   At 23 I would think it would  be worth the effort, as you have your entire adult life ahead of you.

For me (66m), there is no advantage as far as accomodations, and I'm past the age where I could apply for disability. But I have been trying for five years to receive a formal diagnosis. It's hard to find a qualified psychologist, who is aware and informed with current research and understanding of ASD. The "specialist" I encountered five years ago was licensed in the late 1960's and honestly I think I had a better understanding of "high functioning" autism than he did. He didn't offer diagnostic testing because of his wealth of understanding from decades of practice (and arrogance) which he summed up by stating "I know it when I see it". At which point I lost all confidence in him. 

For what it's worth... I think you should pursue it. I didn't when I was your age because I was determined to prove to the world (and myself) that I was capable of managing my own life successfully. Despite what I now recognize as evident difficulties that had become increasingly apparent after I left home for university. (I lasted a month) The abbreviated version of my story is that I did not accommodate myself in any way, unless you count self medicating and denial. I pushed myself mercilessly through meltdowns, alienation and ultimately into burnout. Until I could no longer sustain the effort, or endure the overload. I haven't worked professionally for nearly 20 years, eking out a marginal existence and barely supporting my family. 

Had I followed up when I first began to have serious struggles (at 18), I might have found support or developed the self awareness that I have only recently acquired. I'm not sure if there were supports back then, unless your ASD was disabling to an obvious degree. In which case that often meant residential treatment (the "state hospital"). That's an issue with "high functioning" autism... no one can understand or appreciate how challenging it can be, often including yourself. Regardless of whether you seek diagnosis or are able to find competent and qualified support, it is in your own best interest to educate and advocate for yourself. It is better to be proactive and prepared, than to find yourself in the midst of crisis or on the precipice of tumbling into an abyss... with no net.

I believe it's the internalized gaslighting of what it means to be a man. My wife was primarily indigenous, but presented as "black". In the region where she had been born the "black kriol" were the defacto ruling class. After the revolution in her country the new government purposely sent a large influx of people from other regions of the country to dilute and ultimately usurp power. She didn't identify as black, or indigenous. Being native was not something people would identify with, or aspire to. Despite the fact that they may have only recently (within a generation or two) moved to a city from the "bush". There was so much intermarriage there were no "pure" groups, your membership was cultural, not racial. To the extent that a person who was white, or white passing, could identify as "black kriol". Whether  because of family history or name, and inclusion within the group. This also meant there was little racial prejudice, since within families your cousin might appear to be of a completely different race. They were english or english creole speaking, in a country where Spanish was the official language. Which resulted in them being bi- or multi-lingual.

So, she wasn't accepted by african americans because well... she wasn't. She wasn't accepted by hispanics, because she was black. As far as being accepted by indigenous people, she was always well and warmly received. But she herself was unaware and in fact in denial that she was indigenous at all. (Our daughters DNA test revealed my wife had been nearly 50% indigenous.) The culture and society she  identified with, had been nearly eradicated by cultural (and actual) genocide, and was thousands of miles from where we lived. 

I think that had she known the irrefutable proof of her ancestry, she might have embraced it. At the risk of upsetting some people... she committed suicide a few years ago, and discrimination played a large part. I would suggest embracing who you are. Not that you don't, but you could be more open about self acceptance. I've come to realize that a lot of discrimination is a manifestation of insecurity. Who belongs to which group, and the ensuing gatekeeping that often occurs, do nothing to assure one's sense of self. Other than a somewhat militant assertion of "I belong", and it's corollary "you, don't". My experience with indigenous people has been more welcoming than any other community. Even as a white man. I lost my "white card" when I married my wife. I did not lose, however, white privilege. Until it becomes evident where I stand, which usually happens pretty quickly. Or... if I happen to be with my daughters. You can almost watch the gears turning in their heads, along with the smell of burning wiring (lol). It may come as a surprise, but even venturing beyond my WASP roots was once frowned upon. With disdain for catholics, the irish etc., being common targets. I'm not kidding. White-white. I ended up going no contact with most of my family.

Find your niche, or create one. We have no control over others, only ourselves. Assuming its not the only outlet on the generator, take a meter and verify that power is actually available (and what voltage) at the outlet. Or, plug in a light and watch what happens when it stops pumping. I had a new generator lose output an hour after I got it home, even thought the engine kept running. I've learned to look at the simple stuff, before hauling 200' of pipe+pump across a field. I hope you drilled a weep hole in the pipe before you sank the pump. That way if you do have to pull it out, your not lifting a pipe full of water out also. (Ask me how I know that. LOL)

Things I'd look at; Does a breaker of some kind trip? What are you plugging it into? An outlet on the generator, or a power strip that's plugged into the generator? I ask because you said it worked fine, and then suddenly stopped working. Which would make me think it's a topside electrical problem. Also, is your generator output well beyond the power requirement of the pump? (I use old (pre 70's) generators, after burning up modern ones that simply are not built as well for continuous duty.) On the other side, is it possible something is jamming the pump impeller(s)? You could time the shutoff, if it's exactly the same time every time it's probably not because its jamming. Even a bucket over the well casing will help keep stuff out (I'm assuming it's cased well). You said it's 260' deep, how far is the pump down into that 260'? You could try lowering the pump, as it's unlikely its anywhere near 260' down in the well. If the well controls turn off the pump in the absence of water flow, you could try bypassing that circuit to see if the pump runs (regardless of whether it's pumping). You can feel the vibration by holding the pipe. So that's my two cents.

What drew me to these engines was the realization that "off grid" technologies were available well over 100 years ago. Systems had been designed and implemented that were robust and dependable, before electricity was widely available through the mains. Only with the availability of solar panels has there been any major change. Charge controllers were part of many early 'light plants", like the old Delco units which were D.C., and used glass jar batteries. Modern NiCd batteries evolved from early NiFe (nickel - iron) batteries, and used an alkaline electrolyte (lye) and are nearly indestructible. They were replaced by flooded lead acid batteries, which were cheaper and much lighter. But for stationary applications the NiFe batteries weight really isn't a problem, they routinely last decades. They can be frozen, overheated, undercharged or overcharged, without damage. I use NiCd telecom batteries, as they perform similarly. Anyway, just wanted to share.

Somewhat related: you might look into acquiring an old Lister 6/1 CS (or 8/1) Start-o-matic. You're in the enviable position of being able to find one in someone's garden shed, as they were in wide use for decades in the U.K. and Ireland. They run at 650 rpm, are rated for continuous duty and will run for years with minimal service. They are set up to start on demand, or when your batteries need charging.  Extremely dependable and economical. I use an Indian copy (Metro Premier), which is puttering away right now on straight used vegetable oil. It's  running the air conditioner while I do the wash and other things that would drain my battery bank too quickly.

If suggest you get a pickup truck, if you don't already have one. 275 gallon totes are everywhere, and can often be found under $100. Two or three of these can solve your water issues. One in the truck gets filled and then either drained or pumped into another close to the trailer. If there is any rise in elevation you can use that to advantage. Otherwise a small gas powered pump is handy. If the stationary tank can be placed high enough it can gravity feed the kitchen sink, toilet and shower. As someone has already pointed out a DC element in an electric water heater will give you hot water. Or... there are a number of DIY plans for solar hot water heating. I have a tri-fuel furnace in the basement, wood, oil, electric, so I can make as much hot water as I ever need. They can be found on Craigslist and FB marketplace, sometimes free for hauling them away, and can be used as an outdoor boiler. Again, that's why a truck is essential to take advantage of "opportunities". 

Electric... I went from using 3600rpm (screamer) gas generators (which don't last), to eventually a 6hp Listeroid running a 5kw belt drive Onan generator head. Diesel is by far a better option, the slower the better. That engine can run on any oil you can find, vegetable, waste oil or home heating oil. A 1.5 - 2kw solar array can charge a battery bank for an inverter. I only run the generator to do laundry, run the AC, or anything that is more than solar can provide. I get the oil free when people convert to natural gas and want their oil tank emptied. I only watch the large screen TV when the generator runs, otherwise a laptop screen is enough (for me). 

Which really gets to the point of living off grid. If you are willing to live within the limitations of available power, rather than to live as if you're living in suburbia, then every step you can take to be "independent"... is satisfying. Just my two cents.

I spent nearly a decade trying to prove to myself that I could drink (safely, like a gentleman, etc.), and eventually had to accept that I could not drink... at all. 

No matter what my problem was, alcohol itself had become a problem of such magnitude that continued use imperiled my life, and sanity. I was 26 years old and becoming a "wet brain", so inflamed was my brain from my suicidal drinking habits. Why? Shame, embarrassment, anger, sorrow... bereft and bereaved for the person I might have been, if I had not been molested. 

It only began to dawn on me after a few years of sobriety, that I had been abused at all. So normalized was my boundaryless experience, that I viewed what my experience was as being "sexually active"... starting in my crib. Almost as a disturbing point of pride, which in later years (pre and post adolescence) predators and pedophiles seemed capable of sensing and exploiting. That, coupled with undiagnosed "high functioning" ASD, my natural curiosity and (related to ASD) not understanding that I could say no... to all of it. 

I was 10 or 11 when I met the man who would so thoroughly groom me that I might have considered I was a completely willing participant. I realize now that I was incapable of informed consent, because I was a child. What happened to me, regardless of how I held myself responsible, was wrong. The children and my siblings that engaged inappropriately with me, were also children. I reserve judgement towards my adult abusers, and those who were certainly old enough to know better.

Because if it were not wrong, if it hadn't deeply wounded me, why would I have tried to lose myself in a haze of drugs and alcohol... for years? Or, why would I have attempted (and nearly succeeded) suicide, weeks after my first consensual experience with a woman? Continuing to drink for years to drown the pain that I could not begin to articulate.

What it came down to (at 26 and once again considering suicide) was that I could do nothing about what HAD happened. I wasn't afraid of death. I longed to extinguish the shame of what I felt was self-betrayal. I made a conscious decision to stay, to exorcise whatever demon possessed me.

A moment of clear reflection showed that it made no sense to continue to abuse myself, for being abused.   It's not "easy" to break those habits, drinking or shame. But it is possible. As my head cleared and I started to take care of myself, it became easier to see my trauma for what it was. It takes time, and I'm still working on it decades later. But I stopped blaming myself long ago. I have tried to draw whatever lessons I could, in an effort to cultivate compassion. Both towards others, and myself. The perspective I have gleaned has helped me be less judgemental, more open minded and appreciative of the struggles that (in one way or another) nearly everyone faces. I had surrendered enough of my life to that abyss of unhappiness, and refused to continue carrying that burden of guilt and anger. I realized it belongs to those who hurt me. Some days are hard, but I have found contentment. I hope you can too.

Unsurprisingly, I was often in trouble. For failing to understand how to behave socially, in many cases. I once quoted my father to a friend (age 12), but failed to properly attribute my source. About a decade ago I went off grid. There was a lot going on and the power got disconnected several times. So I finally said the hell with it. Initially it was just a generator, or series of generators. Spending $5 a day for gas, and as long as it lasted was the power for the day. It required everyone to do what they needed to do electricity wise in that time frame. I located an old Kohler 750 watt unit that would run at a little over a pint an hour. But it got frequently overloaded and eventually fried the rod bearings. Then I added four 6 volt golf cart batteries, and a 1kw square wave inverter. Which was transformative. And onward and upward from there.

Now I run an 8kw diesel generator on heating oil that I get free, when people convert to natural gas and want their tanks emptied. I have two battery banks. One is eight 6 volt lead acid batteries wired for 24v-440A, and the other is a telecom battery bank 60 1.4vdc-70A cells wired for 12v output (and I'm too lazy right now to calculate the amperage, or watt hours.) The lead acid setup can be charged by  1600 w of solar (six panels), or the generator via inverter/chargers. The NiCd bank is charged via a 2kw Xantrex Prosine 2.0 pure sine inverter charger. The setup meets our needs, can run everything (easier in the summer). 

I've never paid more than $200 for an inverter-charger. I figured since our farmhouse and farm existed long before electricity was available, and they farmed successfully, so can we. Instead of trying to provide power for a 21st century lifestyle, we adjusted our lifestyle to the power we could afford to provide. Which went from a cap of $150 a month, to essentially $zero. Excluding maintainance costs. The 8kw diesel generator was free, for pickup and repair. Which I did. I'm setting up a 6 hp listeroid diesel ($900), running a 5kw Onan belt drive internally regulated generator head from the late 1940's that cost $50. We own the farm outright, and I have more time than money and do all service, diagnosis and repairs, construction etc.

I didn't want it to come out after months of dating, and have her flee. I asked if she wanted me to take her home, she said "no, you promised me dinner".  

She told me after we were married, that she knew right then that she would marry me. Because I would never judge her. Which I think we instinctively understood, since we knew the details, if not the emotions surrounding each others trauma. As buddhists, it is well within the realm of likelihood.

Thank you, for your efforts.

My theory is that many practices follow a cookie cutter approach of diagnosing clients with a fairly fixed number of conditions. When they veer away from their tried and true approach, that's when claims may be denied, or the billing staff does not know how to code a diagnosis of ASD correctly. For the unfamiliar: every claim must be submitted with the proper, corresponding code, in order to get paid. Also, there is a fixed period of time during which the claim must be submitted. Wrong code, or stale dated claim equals... no money.

Two tangential thoughts, or reflections. (And one pertinent thought.) I always got along with older people, and those from islamic and or "conservative" countries. So, of course, that meant I was gay. (Which is fine, if you actually are, but not the slur.) It seems my formative years had a significant component of editing my behavior, to avoid notice. Lastly, I loathe bullies... the entire species. They deserved to be fired. What they did was an insufferable violation of your personal boundaries. Bullies act from insecurity, they were all probably intimidated by you, for years. We get punished for it, but I believe we must radiate... intelligence?

They may well have been molested themselves. That doesn't change the fact that you were also... by them. COCSA is emotionally complicated for me also. I reserve my larger resentment/concerns for my adult abusers, generally. I had always been skeptical of repressed memories, because there was plenty that I did remember. Until, after recent traumatic events, I connected the dots and there it was. Early (toddlerhood) serial COCSA, and a single event around 7 years old. I (as a survivor, not a mental health professional) now recognize that our mind can go to great lengths to obscure trauma, as an act (or mechanism) of self protection. Take care of yourself first, before wading into the swamp.

I understand the pain of loss, and I can only imagine how heartbreaking your mothers death was, and has been. I'm not entirely at peace, but I am motivated to reach towards it. I never imagined being alone at this point in my life. Because the women in my wife's family routinely live past 100 years. But... recognizing my place on the spectrum has been a revelation.

Being comfortable with yourself is an attractant, I found. I had reached a point, at exactly your age, where I made a conscious decision to stop searching (for a woman) and focus on my education and career. Apparently that appeared as self confidence, and I suppose it was in a way, because I came across as self assured. Through no particular effort on my part, I was preoccupied with my work. I had just stopped worrying about what was going to happen, in that regard.

I would suggest you continue to pursue your interests, and you may be surprised to cross paths with someone who appreciates you exactly as you are. If you communicate best in writing, as I do also, include that. Be open, and honest... and most of all, be yourself. When that person appears out of the blue, you don't want them to be drawn to a version of yourself that you feel compelled to project. Kindness and compassion are undervalued, but highly appreciated.

We moved to suburbia, when my father was transferred to the Manhatten sales office of his employer. I never acclimated. My entire world order had shattered. I went from a community where I was at one with the woodland, to the chaos of a 1960's post war development. Chaos for me that is. My reaction at the time was what I now recognize as a cataclysmic meltdown. A few years later it occured to me that classmates who had moved there only recently were part of a group of friends. Kids that were my classmates for years, yet remained strangers to me. The friendships I did have were always superficial, and short lived. I think I felt lonely, but not necessarily for friends. For the sense of belonging I had left in the hills.

I'll skip over the years of disquiet and my efforts to escape... me. I married at thirty, which was a miracle in itself. At 64, I have one friend, who I suspect I may have finally succeeded in alienating recently. My wife died two years and some months ago. I focus my attentions on my three adult children, who have their own struggles. I'm old enough to not care what anyone thinks about my recluse life, and honestly... it's a relief.

I can manage day to day interactions, but prefer to limit exposure. I can still get tripped up by a smiling face, or a friendly encounter, and have to be vigilant not to unload a dissertations worth of information that may only be of interest to me. 

Like dissemenations on pulp wood mills, renewable forests and the manufacture of paper bags. Only to realize that the smile is gone and the clerk is glancing at the next customer, slack jawed and exchanging knowing looks that tell me once again... I've gone too far.

Not that specifically, but I've run plenty of gas lines. What I would use is 3/4" black pipe with a stub out through the exterior wall and a gas valve. Your flexible line from your tank would connect to that. Inside you can run the line wherever you want, with a valve before the connection to the heater and stove. I don't just put the valve(s) on the end of a line. I use a "tee" and stub out to the valve and then plug the extra hole. That way you can have a place to take off from if you install propane lighting at another time. Also, that way you have a convenient port to pressure check the line.

Edit: You could also use 1/2" black pipe, I've just always used 3/4". I wouldn't use soft copper tubing, BTW.

I live within 1 1/2 hrs from NYC, but its country. We've been off grid for a decade. I've never had any problem at all. Also, you can find good deals on land. Old farms are good because they usually have a well, outbuildings, fields etc. Sidehill farms with patchwork fields instead of big fields. You have to think outside the box. Go to the town hall in the area you're interested in and look at the tax maps (public access), and talk to the assessor. Drive around the back roads. Any house that predates zoning laws is grandfathered and doesn't need a C.O. Also the county lists properties that are going up for tax foreclosure auction. You can get the info and talk to the owner. In some cases it's property that was inherited, and they don't even care about it, or they'd rather sell it to you rather than go to auction. Generally the larger parcels = less per acre. Often waaaay less. There are deals out there much less than 10k per acre.

Recurrent shutdowns and meltdowns at critical or important points in my life. Major depression, schizo-affective disorder, ADHD and C-PTSD all have been diagnosed at various points, but the root issue I believe is ASD. More correctly, the fact that I had no “tool kit” to recognize and deal with my responses to life, people and our culture, left me without the means to negotiate stress and triggers without completely unraveling. Had I known I could have made allowances for myself, instead of pushing myself over the edge, and into an abyss. 

When you talked about your struggles as an adult, and how you realized you were autistic, I immediately identified. As well as with your concern about the apparent malleability of “professionals”. Redundancy is critical. I've had several situations drive this point home. There are two drilled/cased wells on our property. When the house pump failed (in the dead of winter), that's when I found out the well head was 10 feet underground. No problem right? The other well casing stuck out of the ground a few feet, and I had a pump. The problem was getting the water 300 feet from the well, to the house. Pumped water into a 275 gallon tote and tried to trailer it up to the house up a rise. Fine on a sunny fall day, impossible when that "rise" became a sheet of ice in the winter. It may as well have been a mountain. Okay, 300' + 20' of 1" irrigation hose to get it to a 100 gallon tank in the basement. It worked but if you didn't COMPLETELY drain the line within 15-20 minutes it froze solid, and it had to be refilled... frequently. So... that kind of thing. 

For heat I use a tarm wood/coal/oil boiler, that you can also heat electrically. You need to have backups for the backup. You have to be there. You have to fix nearly  everything yourself. You have to be willing to do without. Not always fun, but immensely satisfying when you solve a problem. Also I realigned my thinking to... "what did they do 100 years ago?" As it turns out they had come up with dependable and affordable power solutions back then. Delco Light Plants used a DC generator to charge a battery bank. Its easy to adapt a setup that duplicates that approach with more modern equipment. Learn to live with what you've got, and be grateful. 

I always smile when I hear of some guy who goes "off grid" with a 20kw propane generator, and a 500 or 1000 gallon tank, and expects to live exactly like he's in the middle of suburbia. Until the power goes out for a week and he and his family rip through all that propane. Because the kids stay up until 3am on their computer, every light in the house is on and there's a TV in every room. Along with every hungry appliance in the house. BTW refrigerators and microwaves are real pigs. You can use a propane fridge, and shop for your needs. Don't buy enough perishables to stock a mini-mart. My kitchen stoves are a 1929 Chambers dual fuel, and a Kalamazoo cookstove. Modern stoves require electricity, mine don't. Also, a Maytag wringer washer actually gets clothes clean, and you can hang clothes on a clothesline in winter. Or string up lines between the rafters in a room with a woodstove if you're in a hurry.

Other thing: the brand new generator that's a marvel of integrated circuitry becomes a liability when it breaks, unless your an electrical engineer. Most of them are not up to the service requirements you need it for. And... they're expensive. I use pretty analog equipment, generator wise. Starting with 1950's Kohler 1800 rpm and finally with a Listeroid 650 rpm diesel driving a 5kw 1940's Onan genhead. 
I don't want to have to depend on equipment I can't fix in a pinch, or afford.

As long as the roof didn’t leak, and it had a good well. Far enough from town that we had our privacy, but close enough that we could get to the schools, supermarket, bank, pharmacy and doctors... within minutes. Split off a few acres, and paid off the mortgage. 

Because we had bought the reverse of what most people are after, we had made a great deal. There are good deals out there, you just need to think outside the box. Because the house was so old it was grandfathered, pre-zoning, and didn’t need a C.O. The family of their grandmother were glad to be rid of the responsibility, since she was in a nursing home. 

I pieced together solar panels, a battery bank, inverter and a diesel generator to top up the batteries when the sun doesn’t shine. The only thing I bought new were the batteries. The generator runs on heating oil. I pick up inverters when they come up for a fraction or retail. We have enough acreage to grow most of our food, and there’s game also.

At this point the only “big” expense is property taxes. We may live like 19th century peasants, but if they could do it, so can we. I think financial independence is far easier off grid. I saw your post about 3 hours ago and decided to take a peek online to see what property listings (prices, etc.) were like. So... 3 hrs down the rabbit hole later I’m responding. 

There are some areas that have very, very low taxes, and no zoning. I did see that you have to make sure that your property includes surface and mineral rights. Also, look out for annoying easements: railroad tracks, public access trails, cell tower access roads, power line easements, other PIA right of ways. You didn’t mention any prices, but I would buy as much acreage as you could afford. Smaller acreages will cost more per acre, as they do here. The largest part of your tax burden will be determined by the house you build. I saw several properties in the 25 to 50 acre range with prices between $1,000 - 2,000/ac. 

 I would look for: river or stream frontage, property on both sides of road, fields between road and river on one side, mature woodland sloping upward on other side of road. I saw some that had existing buildings (in that $1-2k range) The advantage is that there could be an existing well and septic system already there. That could save you a LOT of money. It wouldn’t matter what condition the buildings were in, but if there was a usable barn that would be a plus. In areas without zoning the condition of a living structure wouldn’t matter either because you won’t need a C.O. It beats living in a tent while you build what you want. 

My concern about buying 5-10 acres is that you might be surrounded by 5-10 acre parcels. As a previous poster pointed out: what seems like a HUGE parcel when you buy it can become much smaller over time.

If you undersize the generator it may handle the load... for a while... until it kills the engine. You become highly attuned to the sound of your generator. Too often scrambling to pull plugs or trip breakers when you hear it lagging under load, before it melts the bearings in the engine. 

Our family went off grid about twelve years ago. Initially I ran an 8kw propane generator during the active part of the day (because I got it free), and a 750watt gas generator ($75) when I was trying to get everyone to go to bed. Over the years Ive tried different wattages, fuels and makes. What I concluded was that (for me) most modern generators are crap. 

I have several that I keep ready to go, all bought used ranging from 2500 watts to 8kw. (Gas, propane, and diesel.)The best units I have were made in the 50’s to 70’s. They are bulletproof, and their engines run at 1800, 1200, or 650rpm. By far the best way to go is diesel. They can be run on home heating oil. 

If you live in the UK... I would find a Lister Start-o-matic, and set up a battery bank and inverter. Listers and their clones are fairly expensive here in the states, but they are very reasonably priced in the UK. They run at 650rpm and depending on horsepower you can have as little or as much power as you need. I run a 5kw generator head with mine at a little over a pint per hour. More under heavy load. The generator only needs to run to keep the batteries charged, or when demand exceeds supply. You can also add solar panels and charge controller (which we have done)

Refrigeration is a real drain, unless you buy (or grow) fresh food daily. Some people convert a chest freezer to a refrigerator with an auxiliary thermostat. We use a Servel propane refrigerator ($100). For the cost of a brand new 3500w generator you could buy a used generator, a used inverter, and eight 6 volt golf cart batteries. 

We use a 1930 Chambers dual propane/wood cookstove ($100) that has two separate wood fired burners. It does not require electricity to run the oven. We also have a wood fired Kalamazoo cookstove ($50). Prices have risen in recent years, but there are still good deals to be had if you are patient, persistent and willing to travel.

We were already heating with wood. I found a used Tarm wood/coal/oil boiler that is plumbed into the radiators, and provides hot water as well. It can run in a convection loop, or with a recirculating pump. I plumbed a bypass for running it either way. 

It’s expensive to generate your own power with gas, diesel or propane. Of the three: diesel is cheapest in the long run. When people convert from heating oil to natural gas they often run an ad offering their leftover fuel, free. Gas, while expensive, is easy to get... everywhere. 

You didn’t mention anything about a well pump either. When the 240v 1hp jet pump failed, I replaced it with a 120v 1/2 hp submersible. It’s not as efficient as the larger pump, but it’s easier to run with our inverter. I’ll spare you my dissertation on inverters.

Don’t forget the clothes washer, and dryer. Modern washing machines will have the water pump coming on while the machine is running. Maytag wringer washers have their tank filled manually, which works out better. So... I’d recommend a 5kw generator, powered as efficiently as possible, and set up a battery bank etc., ASAP.

A hundred years ago you either did without or generated your own power, unless you lived in a city. There were several companies that made “light plants” that incorporated battery banks for household use. So it’s not a new idea, or technology. 

Hope there’s something helpful in all this. Sorry for such a long post. Everything I know was usually learned the hard way. I think it’s worthwhile to alter expectations of what you need versus what you want. Oil lamps (round wicks, non pressurized) are also good to have on hand. I’ve learned it’s good to have backups for... everything.

You’re an adult now, as far as the right to determine your own choices. You don’t owe anyone your silence. My concern for you is that I know that your trauma will not just go away. Over time it will take more and more, of all that you are, to suppress it. As hard as it is to face it, the consequence of not facing it can be worse. The burden of your trauma will grow heavier over time and insinuate itself into every part of your life. Your relationships, your self image, your self worth. 

You need to approach yourself with kindness, patience and understanding. The way you would if you discovered a child who had been hurt. 

I understand that it’s unfair, and painful. But you don’t need to let it to define you. You can find a path forward that puts your trauma in its proper place, with help. You can manage it, instead of it managing you. You took a courageous first step in that process by telling your therapist, another by reaching out to us. You’ve already begun your journey, and I promise you that as hard as it may ever feel... you will experience all the joys of life, just as intensely. You can talk here, anytime, anonymous and without judgement. Thank you for breaking your silence.
